title: Lakeview Banking - Private VPC Discovery
summary: Discovery focused on Private/VPC deployment requirements: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, CIDR overlap concerns, egress patterns, regional restrictions, KMS/HSM and compliance needs. Agreed next steps: share SOC2 and network runbook, run pilot with a small dedicated VPC, schedule technical deep dive and benchmarks.
action_items: Jordan Mills: Send SOC 2 report + security pack and network runbook (due 2026-03-08)
Priya Kapoor: Draft benchmark plan and sample infra diagram for pilot (due 2026-03-10)
Marta Diaz: Provide VPC CIDR ranges, current peering attachments, and approved egress IPs (due 2026-03-09)
Aisha Nouri: Share compliance checklist items and any reqs for HSM/KMS integration (due 2026-03-11)
next_steps: Redwood to share security + networking docs
Schedule technical deep dive (SE-led) w/ network team next week
Start 4-week pilot in Lakeview test VPC after diagrams agreed
Customer to confirm timeline and stakeholders for procurement
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Mills: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood. With me are Priya our solutions engineer and Sofia from customer success. How's everyone?
[00:12] Tom Reyes: Morning, Jordan. Tom here. We're excited to hear how Redwood could run in our private VPC.
[00:17] Jordan Mills: Awesome. Quick agenda, we wanna understand your network constraints, security/compliance needs, and timeline. Then Priya will go through what Private deployment looks like and what we need from your side. Sound good?
[00:29] Ethan Cole: Yep, that's perfect. We have a couple of specific questions around peering vs PrivateLink and region restrictions — we operate in us-east-1 and eu-west-1.
[00:38] Priya Kapoor: Great, we'll cover both. To start, can you give us a quick overview of your current infra and what you're trying to protect?
[00:45] Tom Reyes: Sure. We're a retail bank, core platform in AWS, most services in us-east-1. We have a VPC per environment (prod/stage/test). Strict egress rules, and we need no data egress to public internet for sensitive PII workloads.
[00:58] Aisha Nouri: Right, and from security, we require that any inference traffic for PII stays within our network or goes over a managed private link. We also need KMS control and audit logs for all requests.
[01:10] Priya Kapoor: OK so the typical options are: Redwood Dedicated in a customer-managed VPC or Redwood Private where we deploy a control plane that can be VPC-isolated. For VPC connectivity we support VPC peering, AWS Transit Gateway attachments, and PrivateLink (interface endpoints). Each has tradeoffs for routing, cross-account peering, and CIDR overlap.
[01:29] Marta Diaz: Quick question — do you require us to open any public egress to reach Redwood control plane?
[01:34] Jordan Mills: No, not necessarily. For Private deployments we can set up VPC interface endpoints using AWS PrivateLink so all control/ingest traffic flows over private endpoints. If you go Dedicated we can also run endpoints in your VPC or in a managed VPC that peers to yours.
[01:48] Ethan Cole: For latency-sensitive requests, we want the inference to be in-region. If we have models served in us-east-1, can you guarantee same-region serving?
[01:56] Priya Kapoor: We can pin routing to region. For Private deployments we deploy inference nodes in the region you pick — us-east-1 is supported. We also provide routing policies; you can set prefer-lower-latency region.
[02:07] Tom Reyes: Ok. On CIDR ranges — we have many legacy VPCs and overlapping ranges with partners. CIDR overlap has bitten us before with peering. How do you handle that?
[02:18] Priya Kapoor: Good call — peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs. If CIDRs overlap, PrivateLink is the safer option because interface endpoints don't require non-overlapping ranges; they use ENIs in your subnet and are reachable via private IPs. Transit Gateway can also help but again requires planning.
[02:33] Aisha Nouri: And about egress IPs — our threat intel team wants a small set of stable egress IPs for allowlisting outbound calls from our network appliances. Does Redwood provide static egress IPs?
[02:44] Jordan Mills: We can provide a set of static egress IPs when using a managed NAT in a Redwood-controlled account or via dedicated egress endpoints. For PrivateLink traffic, egress is within your VPC; for calls that require contacting external services we can centralize egress and provide IP ranges. We'll include a list in the network runbook.
[02:57] Marta Diaz: Is there a requirement to modify route tables or update security groups?
[03:02] Priya Kapoor: For PrivateLink you create interface endpoints in your subnets and update security groups to allow traffic to the endpoint ENIs. For peering you'd update route tables to route to the peered VPC and ensure NACLs permit the ranges. We will provide Terraform modules to make this low friction.
[03:17] Ethan Cole: We also have regulatory constraints — some workloads must remain in eu-west-1. If we need models in multiple regions, do you support multiple private deployments tied to the same account?
[03:27] Priya Kapoor: Yes, multi-region deployments are supported. We can provision inference clusters in each region and the control plane can be configured to route to the nearest region. Each region can be set up with its own PrivateLink endpoints and KMS keys.
[03:38] Tom Reyes: About keys — we need bring-your-own-key (BYOK) and HSM integration for higher risk models. Is that supported?
[03:45] Jordan Mills: We support customer-managed KMS keys and integrations with cloud HSMs for Private deployments. For Dedicated we can arrange HSM-backed key storage; for Private we typically integrate with your KMS in your VPC. We can outline options in the security pack.
[03:58] Aisha Nouri: Audit logs — we need request-level logs retained for 12 months and exportable to our SIEM. How do you handle logs for a private deployment?
[04:06] Sofia Chen: For Private and Dedicated deployments we can stream audit logs to your S3 bucket or into your SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose. Log retention and access controls are configurable; we also support redaction options for PII in traces.
[04:20] Tom Reyes: Good. On network throughput — what kind of bandwidth should we plan per concurrent request? We need to size subnets and NAT accordingly.
[04:29] Priya Kapoor: It depends on model size and token rate. For typical chat workloads with 8k context models, plan for a few megabits per connection. For high-throughput batching, bandwidth needs scale — we'll include sample calculators. For pilot, lowish traffic is fine.
[04:42] Marta Diaz: If we use Transit Gateway for central connectivity across multiple accounts, any blockers?
[04:48] Priya Kapoor: Transit Gateway works well, but you'll need route propagation set up and make sure the TGW is in the same region as the assets or peered across regions. Also consider attachment limits and ensure your security controls attach to the TGW. We can support TGW attachments from our managed account.
[05:01] Ethan Cole: From procurement side, we need clarity on SLA and support — what does Redwood promise for Private deployments?
[05:07] Jordan Mills: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs as part of reserved capacity contracts. Private deployments can be covered via enterprise agreements with support SLAs; we'll loop legal and customer success to propose language.
[05:17] Aisha Nouri: Any hard requirements for outbound ports or DNS? We run strict DNS egress via forwarders.
[05:24] Priya Kapoor: We support private DNS endpoints for service discovery. You can use conditional forwarding to resolve Redwood endpoints to private IPs. For ports, most traffic is HTTPS over 443, but some internal control ports may be required depending on management plane connectivity — we'll list them.
[05:38] Tom Reyes: Can we do mutual TLS between our services and Redwood?
[05:41] Jordan Mills: Yes, mTLS is supported for service-to-service traffic in Private deployments. We also support SAML SSO for the console and RBAC controls.
[05:49] Marta Diaz: If we go live, how is model versioning handled? We want the ability to pin a model and roll forward only after testing.
[05:56] Priya Kapoor: You can pin model versions per route. We support canary rollouts and A/B tests as part of the rollout policies. For Private deployments you maintain control over which models are allowed and when to update.
[06:07] Ethan Cole: Let's talk timeline — ideally we'd run a pilot in 6 weeks and then aim for prod in 12 weeks. Feasible?
[06:14] Priya Kapoor: That's reasonable. Pilot scope: small inference cluster in us-east-1, PrivateLink endpoint, test dataset, 2-4 models for performance checks. After successful bench and security sign-off, expand to prod.
[06:26] Aisha Nouri: For the pilot we'll need the benchmark plan and a network diagram.
[06:30] Jordan Mills: Priya will put that together. We'll also send over the SOC2, penetration test summary, and the network runbook.
[06:38] Tom Reyes: On pricing — is Dedicated pricing a flat reserved fee and Private more custom?
[06:44] Jordan Mills: Yes, Dedicated is reserved capacity pricing (monthly/annual commits). Private deployments are enterprise engagements — platform fee plus support, sometimes with reserved capacity options. We'll send a ballpark after we understand scale.
[06:56] Marta Diaz: Another question — how do you handle software updates for the runtime in Private deployments? We can't have unexpected restarts.
[07:03] Priya Kapoor: We have canary update processes; we coordinate maintenance windows. For critical updates we can schedule with your ops team and ensure rolling restarts with capacity preserved.
[07:12] Aisha Nouri: If we need to run fully air-gapped, is on-prem possible?
[07:17] Jordan Mills: On-prem packages are available for high-regulated customers, though they require a separate engagement. For most customers private VPC with PrivateLink and customer-managed KMS meets requirements.
[07:27] Ethan Cole: Any known gotchas when using PrivateLink with internal load balancers?
[07:31] Priya Kapoor: Make sure the subnets where interface endpoints are created have free IP space for ENIs and that security groups allow the flows. Also watch out for DNS caching; conditional forwarding helps.
[07:43] Tom Reyes: Ok great — can we capture the specific network artifacts we need to provide?
[07:47] Jordan Mills: Yes — we'll need CIDR blocks for the VPC, subnet IDs for endpoints, route table IDs where applicable, security group baselines, and egress allowlist if you want stable IPs. We'll put a checklist in the runbook.
[07:59] Marta Diaz: We'll prepare those. One quick note — we have a corporate proxy that inspects TLS. If traffic goes through that, will it break cert pinning?
[08:08] Priya Kapoor: For mTLS and cert pinning you'll want to route directly to the PrivateLink endpoints and avoid interception; we'll work with your security team to ensure compatibility. If interception is needed, we can advise on trusted proxies and cert management.
[08:22] Aisha Nouri: Lastly — can you guarantee no model data persists outside our VPC?
[08:27] Jordan Mills: For Private deployments we can ensure inference data stays in your VPC boundaries; persistent model artifacts are stored encrypted and can be configured to use your KMS. We'll include exact guarantees in the contract language.
[08:38] Ethan Cole: Ok, sounds good. Anything else from Redwood?
[08:41] Sofia Chen: Just to confirm next steps: we'll send security docs, network runbook, and schedule an SE-led deep dive.
[08:48] Tom Reyes: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[08:51] Jordan Mills: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the action items.
[08:55] End of meeting.
